2.text: child, either on the milk of another suckling woman, if there is any at hand, or

3.text: by feeding it with broth, and, in the Maritime villages, with thin pap pre-
3.note: line-final hyphenation, joins "pared" on line 4; kept as printed

4.text: pared from American flour bought from whalers, which is mixed with a little oil.

5.text: I also gathered among the Asiatic Eskimo, in various villages, some

6.text: curious information about the method which is applied to feed and raise

7.text: babies born prematurely. A baby of this kind is put into the soft skin of a

8.text: big sea-bird. This skin, taken off whole and turned, has the feathers inside.

9.text: Then it is tied up very securely, and hung over a big lamp in which a small

10.text: flame is kept constantly burning. Of course, in doing this, they take care

11.text: that the child’s head shall be in a proper position. In this position the babe

12.text: is kept for from a week to four weeks, during which time it is fed with

13.text: small quantities of oil, as well as with mother’s milk drawn from her breasts.

14.text: Little by little the portion of milk is increased, and at last the babe is allowed

15.text: to suckle. I had no opportunity of witnessing an operation of this kind, but
